explanation:
## The design

```systemverilog
always_comb begin
    int i, k;
    grant = '0;  valid = 1'b0;  pick = '0;
    for (i = 1; i <= N; i = i + 1) begin
        k = (int'(last) + i) % N;
        if (!valid && req[k]) begin
            grant[k] = 1'b1;  valid = 1'b1;  pick = IW'(k);
        end
    end
end

always_ff @(posedge clk) begin
    if (!rst_n)     last <= IW'(N - 1);
    else if (valid) last <= pick;
end
```

One register, `last`, and a rotated priority encoder in front of it.

## The three decisions

**Starting at `last + 1`, not at `last`.** The requester just served
goes to the **back** of the queue. Starting at `last` would let a
requester that keeps asking be served twice in a row while others wait,
which is precisely the starvation the arbiter exists to prevent.

**Assigning defaults first.** `grant = '0; valid = 1'b0;` at the top of
the `always_comb` means every output is assigned on every path. Without
them, the no-requests case leaves the outputs unassigned and the
synthesiser infers a latch — a combinational block that remembers. It
is the single most common bug in SystemVerilog and it does not produce
a warning in simulation.

**Updating `last` only when `valid`.** An idle cycle must not advance
the pointer, or a burst of idle cycles would rotate priority past
everybody and the round-robin guarantee would be about time rather than
about grants. The grading testbench inserts two idle cycles mid-lap and
checks that the next grant is the one that was next.

## Why the loop gives the first and not the last

`if (!valid && req[k])` is the whole of it: once `valid` is set the
remaining iterations do nothing. Written without the guard, every
matching `k` would overwrite the previous one and the arbiter would
grant the position **furthest** after `last` — which is still fair, in
its way, and is not what the specification says.

A `break` would be the obvious alternative. The flag is used here
because it keeps the loop a fixed shape, which is what the synthesiser
unrolls into a fixed amount of logic; `break` is supported, and reading
unrolled hardware out of a loop with early exits is harder.

## What this costs, and the usual alternative

`grant` is combinational, so the path from a requester's `req` pin to
its `grant` pin runs through the whole rotated search: $O(N)$ levels of
logic as written, $O(\log N)$ after the synthesiser rebalances it. For
a 4-way arbiter that is nothing; for a 64-way one it is the critical
path of the design.

The standard fix is to register `grant` and accept that a requester is
served the cycle after it asks. That turns the arbiter into a pipeline
stage, and the protocol above it has to be built to expect the latency.
Which one is right depends on the rest of the system, and the choice is
exactly the one the first bullet of this specification makes.

## The mask trick

A shorter implementation than the loop, and the one you will see in
real RTL:

```systemverilog
wire [N-1:0] mask    = ~((1 << (last + 1)) - 1);   // positions after last
wire [N-1:0] masked  = req & mask;
wire [N-1:0] winner  = |masked ? (masked & -masked) : (req & -req);
```

`x & -x` isolates the lowest set bit. So: look above `last` first, and
if there is nothing there, wrap round and take the lowest requester of
all. Two priority encoders and a multiplexer, with no loop — and
exactly the same behaviour.
